faq.a: Rarely; most cases are bacterial. Viral arthritis usually lacks purulent fluid and high synovial WBC.
Aspiration provides diagnostic fluid and relieves pressure; delaying can cause irreversible cartilage loss.
faq.q: Why is joint aspiration more urgent than imaging?

faq.a: In chronic mono‑arthritis with low‑grade fever, especially in HIV or TB‑endemic regions, and when synovial fluid is paucicellular.

exam: What immediate step should you take in a patient with a hot, swollen knee and fever? — Perform urgent joint aspiration and start empiric IV antibiotics after culture.
How does synovial fluid WBC count help differentiate septic from crystal arthritis? — >50 000 µL strongly suggests infection; crystals may be present but count is usually lower.

A patient with HIV presents with chronic hip pain, low‑grade fever, and a synovial WBC of 10 000 µL. What diagnosis should you consider? — Tuberculous arthritis; obtain acid‑fast stain and culture, start anti‑TB therapy.
Why is cefazolin preferred for MSSA septic arthritis in a low‑resource setting? — It is inexpensive, effective against MSSA, and has a low toxicity profile.
When would you choose surgical arthroscopy over repeated needle lavage? — In deep joints (hip, shoulder) or when drainage is inadequate after two needle attempts.
What red‑flag sign indicates the need for ICU admission? — Septic shock with hypotension unresponsive to fluids.

How can you differentiate septic arthritis from reactive arthritis when the joint fluid is sterile? — Look for recent GI/ GU infection, absence of purulence, and systemic features; consider HLA‑B27 testing if available.
If Gram stain is negative but clinical suspicion remains high, what is your next action? — Continue empiric antibiotics and repeat aspiration; consider PCR or culture on enriched media.
ai.title: Septic (Infectious) Arthritis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Acute bacterial invasion of a joint causes intense inflammation, rapid cartilage loss and risk of systemic sepsis. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Diagnosis requires synovial fluid analysis (cell count, Gram stain, culture) plus clinical picture.
Joint aspiration is the gold‑standard test; do not delay for imaging if the joint is swollen and painful.
sections.p: Septic arthritis is an acute infection of a synovial joint, most often bacterial, leading to purulent synovitis and rapid cartilage destruction.

t.a: Joint aspiration and synovial fluid analysis
t.b: Confirms infection and identifies organism – high WBC (>50 000 µL), neutrophil predominance, positive Gram stain/culture.
If unavailable, start empiric antibiotics after aspiration.
If X‑ray not available, rely on clinical exam and aspiration.
If ultrasound unavailable, use anatomical landmarks for blind aspiration.

b: Mild: localized pain, no fever, normal inflammatory markers.
Moderate: fever, elevated CRP/ESR, joint effusion.
Severe: septic shock, organ dysfunction, rapid cartilage loss on imaging.
sections.p: Severity is judged by systemic response and joint damage; early (≤48 h) vs. established (>48 h) infection guides urgency of surgery.

b: Staphylococcus aureus – most common overall, especially in children and diabetics.
Streptococcus pyogenes – common in children, post‑skin infection.
Gram‑negative bacilli (E. coli, Pseudomonas) – frequent in immunocompromised, urinary source.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis – chronic mono‑arthritis, especially hip/knee in HIV/TB endemic areas.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae – sexually active adults, usually knee.
Candida spp. – rare, in neutropenic or steroid‑treated patients.
sections.p: Bacterial pathogens dominate; epidemiology differs in low‑resource settings.

b: Severe, constant joint pain worsening at night.
Warm, erythematous, tense effusion; joint held in slight flexion.
Fever >38 °C, chills, malaise; may progress to sepsis.
Risk factors: recent skin infection, joint trauma, intra‑articular injection, prosthetic joint, HIV, sickle‑cell disease.
sections.p: The classic triad is joint pain, swelling and limited motion, often with fever and systemic signs.

b: CBC – leukocytosis with neutrophilia.
CRP/ESR – markedly elevated; trend guides response.
Synovial fluid Gram stain & culture – organism identification.
Blood cultures – systemic spread.
X‑ray – joint space narrowing, erosions in late disease.
sections.p: Focused labs and imaging confirm infection and assess severity.

t.b: Elevated in infection but slower to fall; >40 mm/h supports diagnosis.
Distinguishes septic (>50 000 µL) from inflammatory arthritis.

b: Septic shock, hypotension, altered mental status.
Rapid joint destruction → osteomyelitis, ankylosis.
Endocarditis or metastatic infection in bacteremia.
Prosthetic joint infection leading to loosening.
sections.p: Prompt recognition prevents irreversible joint damage and death.

b: Urgent arthrocentesis and lavage; repeat if drainage inadequate.
Empiric IV antibiotics: cefazolin (or cloxacillin) for MSSA; add vancomycin if MRSA risk; consider third‑generation cephalosporin for Gram‑negatives.
Switch to organism‑specific therapy once culture results return.
Adjunctive NSAIDs for pain after infection control; avoid steroids until infection cleared.
Surgical debridement or arthroscopy for hip, shoulder, or refractory cases.
sections.p: Early joint drainage plus targeted antibiotics is the cornerstone.

b: Check CRP/ESR daily; falling trend signals response.
Repeat joint aspiration if no improvement within 48 h.
Educate on wound care, avoid intra‑articular injections without asepsis.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and pneumococcus in high‑risk patients.
sections.p: Monitor clinical response and inflammatory markers; plan long‑term joint care.

b: Crystal‑induced arthritis (gout, pseudogout) – high synovial WBC but negative Gram stain, presence of crystals.
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis – chronic, less acute systemic signs.
Reactive arthritis – follows GI or GU infection, sterile joint fluid.
sections.p: Several non‑infectious arthritides mimic septic arthritis.

b: Negative Gram stain does not exclude infection; culture may be pending.
Normal CRP early in immunocompromised patients.
Low synovial WBC in early TB arthritis; consider TB in endemic areas.
sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening pain, fever >38 °C, hypotension, altered consciousness, or inability to bear weight.
